story_text.value:
Hello HN, I wrote a blog post a while back about not sending me your giant PRs (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49305558). Well, I kept getting huge PRs sent to me, so I've been embraced the AI and let it sweep me away.

Chronosphere rebuilds a PR in logical steps to try to recreate the train of thought that went into the generation of the PR itself. It has github and openrouter integrations for convenience, but can also be used entirely from your current coding agent via a skill integration, no code is uploaded to a central server.

Hopefully this helps you all and your battles to understand mass amounts of AI generated code.

story_text.value:
I started building Aggregate Finance a couple of years ago because I was manually updating a Google Sheet to track my credit card statements, monthly recurring transactions, and spending habits. This seemed perfect for automation as I was having to log in to six separate banking apps to pull this information together.

My original intention was to use this tool locally, but I figured it would be an excellent learning opportunity to understand how to scale the application for others to use. The core functionality of Aggregate Finance revolves around syncing banks and brokerages through Plaid to create visuals and data analytics in Google Sheets and OneDrive/Excel, but I've also added Stripe for payments, passkey and TOTP support for MFA (wanted to better learn how WebAuthn works, mostly), and Resend for emailing account updates.

The first question you're likely thinking is: isn't this just reinventing the wheel? There's plenty of other personal finance/budgeting apps out there like Rocket Money, Monarch, Copilot Money, YNAB, Tiller, Credit Karma, etc. I personally tried Rocket Money but it left a bad taste in my mouth how my entire financial history was stored on their servers without having direct ownership of the data. Another pain point with these personal finance apps is you're locked into their subscription and lose access to your financial data if you cancel.

That's why I opted for the Google Sheet and OneDrive/Excel approach since this persists financial data over time and provides direct data ownership. There's a fair argument that these options still share your financial data with Google or Microsoft, so I built a way to download your financial data locally via CSV/Excel/LibreOffice exports.

In terms of data encryption, Aggregate Finance encrypts financial data before it reaches MongoDB: balances, transactions, merchants, statements, holdings, and any user customizations. Each user gets their own AES-256 key rather than a shared key. The reason I went with this approach is for data deletion: when someone deletes their account, their encryption key is deleted as well, so any financial data stored in prior database backups can't be decrypted.

I've been using Aggregate Finance with my own live bank accounts and investment holdings, and it's already been helpful. I can see when my credit card statements are due, monitor my entire investment portfolio, keep track of recurring charges, create budgets, and see how my spending pans out over a given month or over the past year. I'm curious whether it's useful for anyone else, and I'd of course welcome any feedback on how I can improve it. You can try it with a free sample spreadsheet that contains a year of example data with no bank connection required at https://app.aggregatefi.com.

Hi HN,

I've been working on a bio / visual cortex inspired edge detection algorithm. I released a preliminary version a couple of months ago, and I've been improving it since. Benchmark scores currently sit midway between old-school (Canny, Sobel), and modern deep nets, while having the former's interpretability.

I'm planning to develop this further for downstream use cases, maybe try to improve FPS for video and performance on different hardware.

For anyone interested in a collaboration you can find my email in the Readme. Engineers interested in computer vision frameworks / distributed systems, or anyone in academia following this line of research, feel free to reach out to me.

story_text.value:
On October 26, OpenAI announced a claimed "bare existence" proof in Balaban's RG programme on pure R^4—but notably stopped right before claiming the mass gap Δ > 0. It turns out there is a rigorous mathematical reason why no compute cluster can bridge that gap on flat infinite space.

I wrote a 2,576-line self-contained Lean 4 script (`RoundSquare.lean`) that formally proves a negative-result resolution to the Clay Millennium Yang-Mills problem on pure R^4. In the tradition of Gödel and Turing, it proves that demanding BOTH the full Osterwalder-Schrader/Wightman axioms AND a strict spectral gap Δ > 0 on non-compact R^4 is a structural contradiction.

Bare existence (Δ = 0) satisfies the OS axioms on R^4. But forcing a strict gap (Δ > 0) strictly requires an infrared cutoff via the Gribov horizon and a non-local θ-vacuum projector on the boundary S^3_∞, which immediately destroys Wightman microcausality (Strocchi's theorem) and Wick holomorphicity (GZ complex poles).

The Lean 4 script compiles in 2 seconds with ZERO axioms. No `sorry`, no `Classical.choice`, no `propext`. Every single one of the 74 `#print axioms` checks outputs `does not depend on any axioms`.

While corporate AI labs keep their training data and exact models closed, I believe the future of theoretical physics and millennium-level mathematics must be 100% open-source, machine-verified, and axiom-free.

I've put a 10 LTC bounty on X for anyone who can find a logical flaw in the 74 theorems or exhibit a constructive mechanism on pure non-compact R^4 that generates a strict gap while bypassing the FMR horizon cusps and the S^3_∞ projector.

You can verify the code in your browser without installing anything: 1. Download the script from the URL above. 2. Go to https://live.lean-lang.org 3. Load the file from disk and check the verdicts.

Full preprint with context: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21555360

Would love to hear feedback from the logic and constructive math folks here.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I made this fun app which combines quite a few ideas, I thought you might like the story:

A few months ago I had the idea of looking for anagrams of names. I started with french names using official statistics about first and last names, which also gave me a pretty simple model for likely anagrams: P(first + last) = P(first) * P(last).

Then, I started checking which anagra-names (I coined the term) appeared in the 2021 Facebook leak.

Finally, I improved my ranking using a factorization model.

All this is available as a light and fast webpage thanks to a lot of cool algorithmic tricks detailed here: https://louisabraham.github.io/anagranames/how.html

About the use of AI:

Claude Code was fantastic for building the frontend (including the interactive globe) and writing the MLX code (I would otherwise have used PyTorch, which is slower on my machine). It also handled the quantization with very little guidance, which was particularly useful since I'm not an expert in that area.

That said, I'm glad I learned CS before LLMs existed and still master it enough to work out the ideas and specs for everything else in my head / on paper before handing the implementation over to the agent.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Evan from Gauge. We’re open-sourcing our CLI to recursively improve your docs for coding agents. The CLI includes a local execution backend, so you don't need an account to try it. Explainer video here: https://youtu.be/zhLUlIKB1Mg

The CLI supports a hillclimbing loop:

- set up tasks for coding agents that would need your docs, like 'set up Gauge CI checks'

- run the tasks

- analyze session transcripts for friction or failures

- create variants of your docs to resolve the issues

- re-run the tasks with the doc variants injected (transparently, at the same hostname)

- repeat until you have a variant that resolves the issues

The same loop supports hillclimbing your Skills, CLI, and other agent-facing surfaces.

We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. We were already working with awesome devtool companies, and they were the first ones to ask us how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. We realized this would be something that eventually every company needs to do. Our CLI provides primitives for docs/devrel/eng teams to measure, analyze, and improve how coding agents use their product.

The design boils down to two components: VMs and a network gateway.

The VMs are straightforward, we want the agents to be highly privileged within their environment so that they are representative of developers' coding agents. Each VM generally comes with the agent harness itself, language toolchains, and a git repository.

The network gateway is where we terminate TLS and swap in variants of your docs transparently. The gateway also handles credential replacement, so agents see placeholders and can't exfiltrate keys.

The CLI comes with a 'local' execution backend (inference is still remote). For VMs, it uses Docker containers, and the network gateway is mitmproxy running in a sidecar container for each session.

We've used the hillclimbing loop internally to find and fix coding agent issues like mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. We saw coding agents report that Gauge only supports Claude Code and Codex, traced it back to the web pages they fetched, and fixed the behavior (we support Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity as well). For Clerk, we helped shift coding agents from their legacy 'keyless' mode to their new 'clerk init' command. They were able to validate a pre-release change to their SDK's error messages using Gauge, then saw a 3x increase in coding agents using 'clerk init' post-deploy.

Due to the 'static' nature of AI models, we've realized that closed-loop optimization techniques are now possible for essentially all software products. The same agent can be simulated over and over, meaning that a high-fidelity testing environment is all you need. Achieving the best results boils down to high-quality analysis (finding generalizable friction and objections) and paired experiments (vary only the content, measure the downstream change in behavior).

The repo is here: https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli and you can start using the CLI with: npm i -g @withgauge/cli

We also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cli

If you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix.

We'd love to know from HN: Has anyone tried to DIY this locally, or built something in-house at their company? Is this an improvement? If not, what would need to change?

story_text.value:
Karpathy's HackerTube inspired me to try something similar for datasets. I wanted a place to explore data for project idea and read what people on HN had said about it.

The English version starts with five resources: Common Crawl, OpenStreetMap, Our World in Data, World Bank Open Data, and NYC Taxi Trips. Each has an introduction, metadata, selected HN comments linked to their orginal threads, and related resources found in those discussions.

I started with Chinese version which has a larger and complete catalog. This is a small English edition site to see if you may need or like it. I would continue to expand the resourses pool the same as the Chinese version. Discussion summaries are AI-assisted, with the original comments kept alongside them.

Mentions include criticism as well as praise, so the attention score isn't a recommendation score.

If I've matched a discussion incorrectly or missed something useful about a data resource, please tell me.

It's my first time to build in public and try to collect comments from the famous show on HN channel. I'm willing to receive anything feedback which would be helpful for me and the product.

hits.story_text: I liked the setting in HackerTube (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50319510) that replaces the YouTube thumbnail with a frame from the middle of the video so I had Opus 5.5 build a browser extension to do it for all YouTube videos. Enjoy!
